Central Nervous System
Physiology
Pain Sensation

Pain is a distinct, protective sensation triggered by tissue damage, carried by its own dedicated set of receptors and pathways rather than by overstimulation of other senses. This lesson covers how pain receptors are classified and stimulated, the fast versus slow pain pathways from the spinal cord to the brain, how cutaneous, deep, and visceral pain differ in character and origin, why pain from an organ can be "referred" to a distant skin area, and the somatic, emotional, and autonomic reactions pain triggers, including hyperalgesia.

Characters of Pain

  • Pain is an unpleasant sensation resulting from tissue damage; it triggers protective mechanisms such as the withdrawal reflex or reflex muscle contraction, and drives many people to seek medical advice.
  • Pain is a specific sensation, not the result of overstimulating other sensory modalities.
  • The threshold of excitation of pain receptors is much higher (150 times) than that needed to evoke warmth sensation.
  • Pain is a "pre-potent stimulus" — during pain, other sensations such as hunger or sexual desire are inhibited.
  • Pain receptors adapt very slowly, or not at all.
  • Pain receptors have the widest distribution in the body of any receptor type. The brain itself is not sensitive to pain (it has no free nerve endings); shafts of hair, fingertip skin twigs, liver, and lung parenchyma are also insensitive. The center of the cornea is the most pain-sensitive part of the body.
  • Pain stimuli share the ability to liberate chemical agents that stimulate free nerve endings: histamine, kinins, substance "P", prostaglandins, serotonin, and excess K⁺.

Classification of Pain Receptors

Pain receptors are free nerve endings, subdivided into three types according to their mode of stimulation:

TypeStimulusNerve connection
MechanosensitiveExcessive mechanical stress (crushing, severe trauma)A-delta thin myelinated fibers (5–15 m/sec)
ThermosensitiveExtremes of heat (>45°C) or cold (<10°C)A-delta thin myelinated fibers (5–15 m/sec)
ChemosensitiveChemical injurious stimuliC-fibers, non-myelinated, slowly conducting (0.2–2 m/sec)

Pain Pathway

Fast pain is transmitted by thin myelinated A-delta fibers; slow pain by unmyelinated C-fibers. Both types are branches of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) cells — the first-order neurons. On entering the spinal cord, both fiber types ascend and descend about 3 segments, forming Lissauer's tract, then divide into two systems:

Neo-Spinothalamic Tract (Fast, Sharp Pain)

  • Terminates in laminae I and V (2nd order neuron).
  • Axons cross to the opposite side and ascend to relay in the postero-ventro-lateral nucleus of the thalamus (PVLNT) — the 3rd order neuron.
  • From there, fibers pass through the posterior half of the posterior limb of the internal capsule, then via sensory radiation to somatic sensory areas 3, 1, 2.

Paleo-Spinothalamic Tract (Slow Pain)

  • Terminates in laminae II and III (substantia gelatinosa of Rolando — 2nd order neuron).
  • Axons of the 2nd order neuron cross and join the lateral spinothalamic tract up to the brain stem.
  • Unlike the neo-spinothalamic tract, about 90% of paleo-spinothalamic fibers terminate mainly in: the reticular formation of medulla and pons, the tectal area of the midbrain, and the peri-aqueductal area around the aqueduct of Sylvius.
  • The remaining 10% reach the thalamus (intralaminar and midline thalamic nuclei), then the sensory cortex.

Types of Pain by Site

Cutaneous Pain

Pain from the skin is pricking, stitching, or burning. A sudden injurious skin stimulus produces two distinct phases:

PhaseCharacterFiber & pathwayBlock
ImmediateFast, pricking, well-localized; starts protective reflexesFast myelinated "A" fibers (neo-spinothalamic tract), relay in thalamus then sensory cortexBlocked by moderate nerve compression
DelayedSlow, burning, not well-localized; persists for a long timeUnmyelinated "C" fibers (paleo-spinothalamic tract), relay in reticular formation then all cerebral cortex areasBlocked by local anesthesia

Cutaneous pain is usually accompanied by sympathetic reactions (increased heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, pupil dilatation) and the protective withdrawal reflex.

Deep Pain

  • Arises from deep structures — muscle, ligaments, joints, capsules.
  • Dull, aching, and not well localized; transmitted by "C" fibers.
  • An important example is intermittent claudication, occurring in skeletal muscle due to ischemia or atherosclerosis in old age.
  • Accompanied by reflex muscle spasm, bradycardia, drop in blood pressure, nausea, and even vomiting.

Visceral Pain

  • Free nerve endings in the viscera are far fewer than in skin. Pleura and peritoneum are rich in pain receptors, but liver parenchyma and lung alveoli are devoid of free nerve endings.
  • The sensory cortex is poorly aware of visceral pain: stimuli that cause severe cutaneous pain (a knife cut, cauterization) may cause no visceral pain, while stimuli such as bacterial toxins that cause visceral pain may cause no cutaneous pain.

Causes of visceral pain: over-distension of hollow organs (e.g. stomach), spasm of intestine or ureters, toxins/chemicals in contact with mucosa, ischemia, and traction on the peritoneum or mesentery by a tumor.

Visceral pain is dull, aching, not well localized, sometimes very severe, transmitted by afferent sympathetic or parasympathetic nerve endings (and sometimes somatic afferents), usually accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and bradycardia, and is usually referred to another site.

Referred Pain

Definition: pain felt at a site other than the diseased organ from which it actually originates.

OriginSite of referred pain
Anginal pain (cardiac ischemia)Retrosternum, medial side of left arm with little finger, jaw or root of the neck, back of left scapula
Gall bladder painTip of right shoulder
Renal painTesticles and loin
Appendicular painUmbilicus and epigastrium
Uterine and labor painThe back

Mechanisms of Referred Pain

  • Branching dorsal root theory: pain from the viscera and pain from a certain area of skin both enter the spinal cord through the same dorsal root. The cortex is conditioned to interpret impulses from that root as coming from the skin (since the brain is not normally aware of the viscera), so referred pain follows the dermatomal distribution.
  • Convergence-projection theory: visceral pain fibers entering through one dorsal root converge onto the same dorsal horn cell as normal sensations from a skin area entering through a different dorsal root. Because most pain reaching the cortex from that neuron normally comes from the skin (the organ regularly exposed to trauma), the cortex projects the sensation as if it originates from the skin.

Reactions to Pain

Although the pain threshold is the same in all individuals, people differ greatly in their reactions to pain.

1. Somatic Reflexes

Painful stimuli cause reflex skeletal muscle contraction (withdrawal), which removes the person from danger. Muscles overlying a painful area — such as an inflamed appendix — reflexly contract, producing "guarding rigidity" that can make clinical examination difficult; bone fracture is likewise associated with severe muscle spasm. Mechanism: pain-carrying nerve fibers give collaterals, on entering the spinal cord, to the anterior horn cells that innervate the surrounding muscles.

2. Emotional Reactions

Pain impulses reaching the sensory cortex send collaterals to the hypothalamus (a higher emotional center), producing reactions such as crying, anger, or depression. Very severe pain may even cause complete loss of consciousness or fainting.

3. Autonomic Reactions

Caused by impulses reaching the reticular formation from ascending pain fibers: changes in heart rate, respiratory rate, pupil dilation, sweating, and even inhibition of GIT activity. Mild pain generally causes sympathetic stimulation, while very severe or visceral pain stimulates parasympathetic activity; marked blood pressure changes may also occur.

4. Hyperalgesia

Definition: a pathological skin state in which normally non-painful stimuli become painful, because the threshold of pain receptors is markedly lowered.

TypeLocationMechanism
Primary hyperalgesiaAt the site of the lesion itself — edematous, red, hot, very painfulLocal axon reflex: destroyed tissue releases mediators that lower the receptor threshold, cause local vasodilatation, and produce antidromic impulses causing arteriolar dilation; resulting edema maintains pressure on hypersensitive nerve endings
Secondary hyperalgesiaIn the surrounding area of the lesion — falsely appears normal, but strong stimulation induces severe painConvergence-facilitation theory: sensory nerves from the primary area converge on a spinal neuron, which becomes "facilitated" with abundant chemical transmitter; painful sensation reaching this neuron from the secondary area is then transmitted to the sensory cortex as very painful

Key Points / Quick Review

Characters of Pain

  • Distinct, pre-potent sensation; inhibits other sensations during acute pain
  • Pain threshold ≈150× higher than warmth threshold
  • Very slowly adapting or non-adapting
  • Brain, hair shafts, liver and lung parenchyma: insensitive; cornea: most sensitive
  • Chemical mediators: histamine, kinins, substance P, prostaglandins, serotonin, K⁺

Receptor Classification

  • Mechanosensitive & thermosensitive → A-delta fibers (5–15 m/s)
  • Chemosensitive → C fibers (0.2–2 m/s)

Pain Pathways

  • Neo-spinothalamic: fast pain, laminae I & V → PVLNT → areas 3,1,2
  • Paleo-spinothalamic: slow pain, laminae II & III; 90% to reticular formation/tectum/periaqueductal grey, 10% to thalamus

Cutaneous Pain

  • Fast pricking ("A" fibers) — blocked by nerve compression
  • Slow burning ("C" fibers) — blocked by local anesthesia

Deep & Visceral Pain

  • Deep pain: dull, "C" fiber; intermittent claudication is a key example
  • Visceral pain: caused by distension, spasm, ischemia, traction — not by cutting

Referred Pain

  • Angina → left arm/little finger/jaw/scapula; gall bladder → right shoulder; renal → testicles/loin; appendix → umbilicus/epigastrium
  • Explained by branching dorsal root theory or convergence-projection theory

Reactions & Hyperalgesia

  • Somatic (withdrawal/guarding), emotional (via hypothalamus), autonomic (via reticular formation)
  • Primary hyperalgesia: at lesion site, local axon reflex
  • Secondary hyperalgesia: surrounding area, convergence-facilitation
